title: Ragtime Won the Tony Last Night. A Musical About Immigrants and the American Dream Hit Different This Year.
excerpt: Pink opened with Lady Marmalade, John Lithgow picked up his third Tony at 80, and Broadway closed its biggest season ever. The night belonged to stories about who gets to belong.
body:
The 79th Tony Awards began with a spectacle and ended with a statement.

**Pink** — pop star, acrobat, and apparently a lifelong Broadway devotee — opened the ceremony at Radio City Music Hall with a seven-and-a-half-minute rendition of "Lady Marmalade" that involved every nominated musical cast on stage simultaneously. Her daughter Willow had convinced her to take the hosting gig. "There will be stunts," she told reporters beforehand, "and not just for me."

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZSvGQkymEP/

https://www.instagram.com/reel/DZSvGQkymEP/

But the night's real stunner wasn't airborne. It was **Ragtime**, the sweeping revival of the 1998 musical that interweaves the lives of Black, immigrant, and upper-class white families in early twentieth-century America — a story about race, class, aspiration, and the savage promise of the American Dream. It beat out the wildly inventive **Cats: The Jellicle Ball** for Best Revival of a Musical, and its stars swept the leading performance categories: **Joshua Henry** won Best Actor in a Musical for his searing turn as Coalhouse Walker Jr., and **Caissie Levy** took Best Actress for her portrait of Mother, the privileged woman whose world cracks open when she confronts injustice.

> "Antisemitism, cruelty of all kinds... these are things that we're dealing with these days up front and personal." — John Lithgow, accepting his third Tony

The evening's acting honors were equally commanding. **John Lithgow**, at 80, won Best Actor in a Play for **Giant**, Mark Rosenblatt's drama about Roald Dahl confronting the fallout from his antisemitic remarks. It was Lithgow's third Tony — his first came 53 years ago for *The Changing Room*. And **Lesley Manville** was devastating as Jocasta in Robert Icke's **Oedipus**, a reimagining of Sophocles as a taut political thriller that earned her Best Actress in a Play.

On the new play front, **Liberation** — **Bess Wohl's** drama examining the legacy of the 1970s women's movement — added the Best Play Tony to its 2026 Pulitzer Prize. Wohl became only the fourth woman to win the award, and the first since 2009.

**Laurie Metcalf** picked up her third Tony for Best Featured Actress in a Play as Linda Loman in Joe Mantello's revival of **Death of a Salesman**, opposite **Nathan Lane**. Metcalf revealed she had deliberately never watched a production of the play, saving it for the day she'd be in one herself. That revival was the night's most decorated production, winning six Tonys including Best Revival of a Play and Best Direction for Mantello.

The new musicals delivered their own brand of spectacle. **The Lost Boys** — a stage adaptation of the 1987 vampire cult classic — earned **Shoshana Bean** her first Tony for Best Featured Actress after three nominations, alongside **Ali Louis Bourzgui** for Best Featured Actor. Bean's speech was the night's most emotional moment. "This is for the single mamas," she said. "You are the wild heroes. Be free, be loud, be great."

**Schmigadoon!**, based on the Apple TV+ series, led the craft categories with three wins including Best Original Score and Best Book, both for creator **Cinco Paul**. And **Cats: The Jellicle Ball** — a radical reimagining of Andrew Lloyd Webber's musical set in New York's ballroom culture — won Best Direction and Best Choreography, with directors **Zhailon Levingston** and **Bill Rauch** delivering a tag-team acceptance speech that honored "the Black and Brown trans women and gay men who were ballroom's pioneers."

The ceremony capped a record Broadway season that generated **$1.91 billion** in gross revenue — the highest in the industry's history. For the millions in the Indian diaspora who make theater a regular cultural outing in New York, Chicago, London, and Toronto, the message was unmistakable: Broadway isn't just surviving the streaming age. It's thriving in it.

And Ragtime's message — that the immigrant experience in America is beautiful, violent, hopeful, and still unresolved — landed with the force of a story that could have been written yesterday. If you're anywhere near a Broadway theatre this summer, this one isn't optional.
